title: Simple rational modules of split semisimple groups remain simple after field extension
statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field] and let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. Assume $G$ is semisimple: after algebraic closure it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, with solvable meaning that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial. Assume $G$ has a split maximal torus, meaning a closed subgroup isomorphic to a finite product of $\mathbf G_m$, maximal among tori after algebraic closure; $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$. Let $V$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional rational $G$-representation [def-wf-algebraic-representations]. Simple means that the only $k$-linear subspaces preserved by the action after every commutative $k$-algebra extension are $0$ and $V$. If $V$ is simple, then for every field extension $K/k$ [def-pc-field-extension] the scalar-extended representation $V_K=K\otimes_kV$ of $G_K=G\times_kK$ is simple: its only $K$-linear subspaces invariant after every commutative $K$-algebra extension are $0$ and $V_K$.

source.place: 22.2--22.4, printed pp.463--464, especially 22.4: End(V(lambda))=k and simplicity after extension; supporting scalar-extension criterion 4.19(b), printed pp.90--91.

proof.text: Choose a split maximal torus $T\subseteq G$ from the hypothesis. Apply [lem-sfb-split-simple-multiplicity-one-weight] to this $T$ and the given simple rational $G$-module $V$. Its hypotheses are exactly smoothness, connectedness, affineness, finite type, geometric semisimplicity, split maximality of $T$, and finite-dimensional simplicity, all assumed here. Obtain a character $\lambda:T\to\mathbf G_m$ and a nonzero $v\in V_\lambda$ with $V_\lambda=kv$.

Let $f:V\to V$ be any rational $G$-equivariant endomorphism. For every $k$-algebra $A$ and $t\in T(A)$, equivariance gives $t(1\otimes f(v))=(1\otimes f)t(1\otimes v)=\lambda(t)(1\otimes f(v))$. Thus $f(v)\in V_\lambda=kv$, so $f(v)=av$ for some $a\in k$. Put $q=f-a\,\mathrm{id}_V$ and $N=\ker q$. The space $N$ is rationally invariant: for every $A$, a basis of $N$ extended to a basis of $V$ identifies $A\otimes_kN$ with $\ker(1\otimes q)$ (the independent images under $q$ of a basis of a complement remain independent after tensoring). Equivariance of $q$ then preserves this kernel under every $g\in G(A)$. Since $v\ne0$ lies in $N$, simplicity forces $N=V$, hence $f=a\,\mathrm{id}_V$. Conversely, scalar maps commute with every action. This proves the precise scalar-endomorphism hypothesis needed in the next step over $k$, without assuming $k$ algebraically closed.

source.place: 22.4, p.464 and Exercise 22-1, p.482; explicit kernel argument as in the proof of Schur Lemma 4.20, p.91.

proof.text: Fix any field extension $K/k$. Apply [lem-sfb-scalar-endomorphisms-absolute-simplicity] with $H=G$ and the original representation $V$. The original hypotheses supply finite type, affineness, finite-dimensionality, nonzeroness and simplicity. Step 2 supplies every rational equivariant endomorphism being scalar, in the sense of commuting with the action after every commutative $k$-algebra extension. The criterion gives simplicity of $K\otimes_kV$ as a rational $G_K$-module, with invariance tested after every commutative $K$-algebra extension. This is precisely the required conclusion, for arbitrary $K/k$.

proof_origin.place: 22.2--22.4, pp.463--464, and 4.19(b), pp.90--91; scalar endomorphisms proved using the multiplicity-one weight and the elementary kernel argument of 4.20.
